screens.title: Network Address Translation (NAT)
screens.narratorSegment: Network Address Translation is a pragmatic solution that lets private networks use non-routable addresses while communicating on the public internet. In practice, NAT conserves scarce IPv4 addresses and obscures internal topology by translating between inside local addresses and inside global addresses. You will learn the address role names, how a router uses ip nat inside and ip nat outside to decide which packets to translate, and the three operational patterns: Static NAT for stable one-to-one mappings, Dynamic NAT that borrows addresses from a pool, and PAT which overloads a single public address using unique source ports. Knowing when to use each type is critical: servers that must be reachable externally usually need Static NAT, small groups of hosts can use Dynamic NAT when limited public addresses are available, and most user internet access uses PAT for scale. This lesson also prepares you to configure, verify, and troubleshoot NAT on Cisco routers using commands like show ip nat translations and clear ip nat translation. By the end you will be able to map requirements to NAT types and reason about common misconfigurations that prevent translations. Think about a web server you must make reachable from the internet — NAT gives you a predictable public identity while keeping the server on a private network.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Network Address Translation
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Network Address Translation

Conserve IPv4 addresses and provide an address boundary between inside and outside networks. Learn address roles, NAT types, and configuration essentials.

Why it matters
NAT reduces public IP consumption and makes internal addressing flexible while giving external presence when needed.
What you'll practice
Static mappings for servers, dynamic pools for power users, and PAT for general user internet access.
Explore Key Topics
Static NAT
Permanent one-to-one mapping for servers requiring stable public addresses.
Dynamic NAT
Many-to-many mapping that borrows addresses from a public pool when needed.
PAT / NAT Overload
Many-to-one mapping using source ports so many hosts share a single public IP.
Concept map
Inside Local
Private IP used by internal host.
Inside Global
Public IP used to represent the internal host externally.
Outside Local
External host's address as seen from inside.
Outside Global
External host's public address on the internet.
Orientation

This lesson series will move from concept to configuration to verification and troubleshooting, ending with a hands-on router template you can adapt. Keep an eye on interface roles and access lists — they determine what traffic gets translated.

Static, Dynamic, PAT

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will build a practical skill set around NAT. First, you will explain why NAT is used and identify the address roles such as inside local and inside global. Second, you will differentiate Static NAT, Dynamic NAT, and PAT so you can pick the correct strategy for servers, power users, and general hosts. Third, you will configure Static mappings and Dynamic pools on a Cisco router, and implement PAT using the overload keyword. Finally, you will verify and troubleshoot NAT with show and debug commands. Each objective includes hands-on practice: for example, configuring a Static NAT mapping for a web server and verifying reachability. You'll also practice creating ACLs used for dynamic pools and PAT. These competencies matter because NAT influences connectivity and security at the network edge; mistakes commonly come from incorrect interface designations or ACL mismatches. By the end you will recognize configuration errors, interpret translation tables, and restore correct operation. This set of objectives prepares you to implement address translation reliably in production networks while conserving IPv4 addresses and maintaining predictable server presence.

screens.title: What NAT does and why it matters
screens.narratorSegment: Network Address Translation translates addresses used inside a private network into addresses usable on the public internet. The practical effect is twofold: it conserves IPv4 addresses and it separates internal addressing from the externally visible address space. For example, a company with thousands of devices can assign private addresses like 192.168.0.0/16 internally and use a small set of public addresses only when hosts initiate external sessions. This avoids the need to request a public address for every internal host. NAT also provides a modest layer of obscurity: external systems see the inside global addresses rather than the internal topology. That does not replace proper security controls, but it reduces direct exposure of internal hosts. Definition matters when choosing a strategy. Static NAT is a permanent one-to-one translation used when an internal service must be reachable by a stable public address. Dynamic NAT borrows addresses from a pool, which is useful when a subset of users occasionally need public addresses. PAT, or NAT Overload, multiplexes many internal hosts onto a single public IP using different source ports, which is why PAT is the dominant model for general internet access. A common misconception is that NAT is a security control — while NAT can hide internal addresses, it is not a substitute for firewalls and access controls. Consider how a web server keeps a known public presence via Static NAT: that predictability is the primary reason to choose static mapping for servers. How would you match your use case to one of these three types?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: NAT maps private addresses to public addresses to conserve IPv4 and present a controlled external identity.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › What NAT does
Definition

NAT purpose and effect

NAT conserves public IPv4 addresses and hides internal addressing by translating inside local addresses to inside global addresses when communicating externally.

Concrete example
A campus uses 192.168.0.0/16 internally and a handful of public addresses for external access; NAT translates host sessions to the public pool when needed.
Common misconception
NAT hides addresses but is not a replacement for firewalls. Do not rely on NAT alone for perimeter security.
Key Takeaway

NAT provides address conservation and a controlled externally visible identity, but security still needs dedicated controls.

Analogy
Think of NAT like a receptionist who forwards calls: many internal people have private extensions, but the receptionist uses a small set of public numbers to reach the outside world and returns calls to the correct extension.
Why this matters
  • Conserve scarce IPv4 addresses across many devices.
  • Give servers a stable public identity with Static NAT.
  • Scale user access with PAT by multiplexing on source ports.
Try this
List which hosts in your network need fixed public addresses and which can use PAT. That list guides whether to apply Static, Dynamic, or PAT.

screens.title: NAT address terminology
screens.narratorSegment: NAT uses specific names for the addresses involved in translation — learning these terms prevents confusion when designing and troubleshooting translations. Inside Local refers to a private IP assigned to a host within the internal network. Inside Global is the public IP that represents that internal host when it communicates externally. Outside Local is how an external host appears to the inside network; this could be unchanged or translated depending on the topology. Outside Global is the external host's public address on the internet. For example, an internal web server might be Inside Local 192.168.1.10; when you create a static mapping to 203.0.113.10, that public address is the Inside Global. If an internal client accesses an external service, the remote server's public address is the Outside Global and the router may show that same address as Outside Local to inside hosts. Misreading these roles often leads to troubleshooting errors, especially when examining show ip nat translations output. Remember: 'inside' and 'outside' are relative to the router performing NAT. A frequent mistake is assuming inside and outside always map to physical interfaces by name; instead verify which interfaces are tagged with ip nat inside and ip nat outside before relying on translations. How would you label the addresses in your network for clarity?

keyIdea.title: Terminology
keyIdea.text: Inside/Outside and Local/Global distinguish where an address is used and how it appears externally.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Address Terminology

Address Roles

These labels reduce ambiguity when you inspect translation tables or design NAT policies.

Inside Local
Private IP used by an internal host, not routable on the internet.
Inside Global
Public IP assigned to represent the inside host externally.
Outside Local
How an external host appears to the inside network. Can vary with topology.
Outside Global
The public address of an external host on the internet.
Concrete example
Inside Local 192.168.1.10 mapped to Inside Global 203.0.113.10 via Static NAT for a publicly reachable server.
Misconception check
Do not assume 'global' always equals 'outside interface address'. Inside Global may be a pool address or interface IP depending on configuration.

screens.title: Designating interfaces: ip nat inside / ip nat outside
screens.narratorSegment: The router must know which interfaces face the internal and external networks to apply NAT correctly. The commands ip nat inside and ip nat outside tag interfaces so the NAT engine treats packets according to their direction. When an internal host initiates a connection to the internet, the packet arrives on an interface marked as inside; the router consults translation rules and either applies a static mapping, assigns an address from a dynamic pool, or performs PAT using the outside interface address with overload. If these interface tags are reversed, translation never occurs. For example, if you accidentally set the WAN-facing interface to ip nat inside, the router will not translate outbound traffic as expected and show ip nat translations will be empty. A straightforward process to avoid this error is to confirm interface addresses and then apply the ip nat keywords: set the inside-facing interface connected to 192.168.1.0/24 as ip nat inside and the outside-facing interface connected to 203.0.113.0/24 as ip nat outside. After configuration verify translations by initiating traffic and using show ip nat translations. A common troubleshooting step is repeating the interface checks first, because incorrect interface roles are among the most frequent causes of NAT failure. What would you check first if translations never appear?

keyIdea.title: Interface roles
keyIdea.text: Correctly mark inside and outside interfaces to let the router apply NAT rules to the right packets.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Interface Roles
Process

Set interface roles

Tag the internal interface with ip nat inside and the external interface with ip nat outside before applying NAT source rules.

interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 192.168.1.1 255.255.255.0
 ip nat inside
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 203.0.113.1 255.255.255.0
 ip nat outside
Example check
If show ip nat translations is empty but clients can reach the internet, ensure interface roles are correct; swapped roles prevent expected translations.
Why order matters
  • The router applies NAT translations based on configured rules and the packet direction determined by interface roles.
  • Set roles first, then create ACLs, pools, and source mappings so rules operate on correct traffic.
  • Mis-applied roles are the most frequent configuration error and easy to verify and fix.
Pro tip
Document which interface connects to inside and outside networks before applying NAT; diagram the flows to avoid role confusion.

screens.title: Static NAT configuration
screens.narratorSegment: Static NAT creates a permanent one-to-one mapping between an inside local IP and an inside global IP. Use this when an internal host, like a web or email server, must keep the same public address so external clients can reach it reliably. The configuration pattern sets the inside and outside interface roles, then applies ip nat inside source static. In the example from the chapter, the server 192.168.1.10 is mapped to 203.0.113.2. After creating the static mapping, incoming packets destined for 203.0.113.2 are translated and forwarded to the internal server. A common pitfall is forgetting to tag the router interfaces correctly; if ip nat inside is missing on the LAN interface or ip nat outside is missing on the WAN interface, the translation will not occur. Another mistake is overlapping mappings that conflict with dynamic pools or PAT rules; keep static mappings distinct. When verifying, use show ip nat translations to confirm the static entry and test external access to the public IP. A misconception is thinking Static NAT affects outbound source addresses for client connections; static mappings primarily ensure inbound reachability to the internal host. How would you prioritize static mappings when you also need a dynamic pool and PAT on the same router?

keyIdea.title: Static mapping
keyIdea.text: Static NAT gives a stable public identity to an internal host, essential for servers that must be reachable externally.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Static NAT
Configuration Example
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 192.168.1.1 255.255.255.0
 ip nat inside
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 203.0.113.1 255.255.255.0
 ip nat outside
!
ip nat inside source static 192.168.1.10 203.0.113.2
This mapping ensures that requests to 203.0.113.2 are forwarded to 192.168.1.10 consistently.
Explanation & Tips
  • Static NAT is ideal for servers that need a persistent public address.
  • Verify with ping and show ip nat translations; static entries should appear and persist.
  • Avoid address overlap with dynamic pools or PAT target addresses.
Common mistake
Applying ip nat inside/outside incorrectly will prevent the mapping from being used; always confirm interface tags.

screens.title: Dynamic NAT configuration
screens.narratorSegment: Dynamic NAT creates an on-demand mapping between eligible inside hosts and a pool of public IP addresses. Unlike Static NAT, mappings are temporary and only exist for the duration of a session. To configure Dynamic NAT you define a standard ACL identifying the inside addresses that may be translated, then declare an ip nat pool with the public addresses and netmask, and finally bind them with ip nat inside source list pool. In the chapter example, hosts in 192.168.1.0/24 can be dynamically assigned addresses from 203.0.113.10 through 203.0.113.15. If the pool is exhausted, subsequent internal requests fail until an address is freed. This limitation distinguishes Dynamic NAT from PAT, which can scale more densely. A common configuration error is a mismatched netmask for the pool or ACL too narrow or too broad; these mistakes either prevent translations or translate unintended hosts. For verification, watch show ip nat translations during session initiation to observe pool addresses assigned. A practical misconception is expecting Dynamic NAT to provide inbound stable access — it does not guarantee the same public IP is available for return traffic, so do not use it for servers that require consistent reachability. Would a small team of power users benefit more from Dynamic NAT than PAT? Consider pool size against concurrency.

keyIdea.title: Dynamic mapping
keyIdea.text: Dynamic NAT assigns public addresses from a pool for the duration of sessions; it is temporary and limited by pool size.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Dynamic NAT
Configuration
ip access-list standard NAT_POOL_ACL
 permit 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255
!
ip nat pool PUBLIC_IPS 203.0.113.10 203.0.113.15 netmask 255.255.255.248
!
ip nat inside source list NAT_POOL_ACL pool PUBLIC_IPS
Hosts matching the ACL will be allocated a public address from the pool when they initiate outbound connections.
Operational notes
  • Pool exhaustion prevents new translations; size the pool for peak concurrency.
  • Dynamic NAT does not provide a stable public identity for inbound access.
  • ACLs must accurately match inside hosts; overly broad ACLs translate unintended traffic.
Misconfiguration
Using the wrong netmask for the pool will cause address mismatches and unexpected behavior; double-check mask values.

screens.title: Port Address Translation (PAT)
screens.narratorSegment: Port Address Translation, commonly called PAT or NAT Overload, enables many internal hosts to share a single public IP address by differentiating sessions with unique source ports. To configure PAT you create a standard ACL that matches internal hosts, then use ip nat inside source list interface overload. The overload keyword signals the router to reuse the outside interface IP and vary source ports to maintain session uniqueness. In the chapter example, all hosts in 192.168.1.0/24 appear externally as 203.0.113.1 while the router tracks port mappings to maintain separate connections. PAT is highly scalable for general internet access, but it does not give an internal host a stable public identity; it is unsuitable for servers that need inbound connections mapped to them. A common error is omitting overload, which results in dynamic NAT behavior that can exhaust pool addresses quickly. When verifying PAT, use show ip nat translations to inspect port mappings and statistics. Misconceptions include assuming PAT hides all internal details; while it hides internal IPs, port-level mappings still reveal session endpoints. How would you balance PAT for general users and Static NAT for servers on the same router?

narration.text: Port Address Translation, commonly called PAT or NAT Overload, enables many internal hosts to share a single public IP address by differentiating sessions with unique source ports. To configure PAT you create a standard ACL that matches internal hosts, then use ip nat inside source list interface overload. The overload keyword signals the router to reuse the outside interface IP and vary source ports to maintain session uniqueness. In the chapter example, all hosts in 192.168.1.0/24 appear externally as 203.0.113.1 while the router tracks port mappings to maintain separate connections. PAT is highly scalable for general internet access, but it does not give an internal host a stable public identity; it is unsuitable for servers that need inbound connections mapped to them. A common error is omitting overload, which results in dynamic NAT behavior that can exhaust pool addresses quickly. When verifying PAT, use show ip nat translations to inspect port mappings and statistics. Misconceptions include assuming PAT hides all internal details; while it hides internal IPs, port-level mappings still reveal session endpoints. How would you balance PAT for general users and Static NAT for servers on the same router?

keyIdea.title: PAT behavior
keyIdea.text: PAT maps many private addresses to one public IP using unique source ports for each session, maximizing address efficiency.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › PAT / NAT Overload
PAT Configuration
ip access-list standard PAT_ACL
 permit 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 203.0.113.1 255.255.255.0
 ip nat outside
!
ip nat inside source list PAT_ACL interface GigabitEthernet0/1 overload
All hosts matching PAT_ACL will share 203.0.113.1 with unique source ports distinguishing each session.
Notes & pitfalls
  • Include the overload keyword to enable many-to-one behavior; omitting it triggers dynamic NAT semantics.
  • PAT scales well for outbound client traffic but is not appropriate for hosting externally reachable services.
  • Verify port mappings with show ip nat translations when diagnosing session collisions or port exhaustion issues.
Key Takeaway
PAT efficiently conserves addresses by using port multiplexing, making it the default for general internet access.

screens.title: Choosing between Static, Dynamic, and PAT
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the correct NAT type depends on whether hosts need stable public identities, how many concurrent public addresses you have, and how you prioritize scalability. Static NAT offers a predictable one-to-one mapping and is appropriate for servers that must be reachable externally, but it consumes one public IP per mapped device. Dynamic NAT conserves addresses by using a pool and assigns them only during sessions, making it suitable for a small group of power users who occasionally need public addresses; it requires careful pool sizing because once the pool is exhausted new sessions fail. PAT is the most scalable option for general user internet access because many inside hosts share a single public IP using distinct source ports, but it does not provide stable inbound reachability. When deciding, list the services that require inbound connections, estimate concurrent outbound sessions, and calculate whether your public IP pool can support the expected concurrency. A common misconception is that Dynamic NAT and PAT are interchangeable; they are not — Dynamic NAT provides a public address per session from the pool, while PAT multiplexes on a single IP with port differentiation. For practical planning, place static mappings first for servers, allocate a small pool for special users with Dynamic NAT, and enable PAT for the remainder. How would you size the pool if you expect ten simultaneous power-user sessions?

narration.text: Choosing the correct NAT type depends on whether hosts need stable public identities, how many concurrent public addresses you have, and how you prioritize scalability. Static NAT offers a predictable one-to-one mapping and is appropriate for servers that must be reachable externally, but it consumes one public IP per mapped device. Dynamic NAT conserves addresses by using a pool and assigns them only during sessions, making it suitable for a small group of power users who occasionally need public addresses; it requires careful pool sizing because once the pool is exhausted new sessions fail. PAT is the most scalable option for general user internet access because many inside hosts share a single public IP using distinct source ports, but it does not provide stable inbound reachability. When deciding, list the services that require inbound connections, estimate concurrent outbound sessions, and calculate whether your public IP pool can support the expected concurrency. A common misconception is that Dynamic NAT and PAT are interchangeable; they are not — Dynamic NAT provides a public address per session from the pool, while PAT multiplexes on a single IP with port differentiation. For practical planning, place static mappings first for servers, allocate a small pool for special users with Dynamic NAT, and enable PAT for the remainder. How would you size the pool if you expect ten simultaneous power-user sessions?

Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Choose NAT Type
Static NAT
Pros: Predictable inbound access. Consumes one public IP per host. Use for servers.
Dynamic NAT
Pros: Temporary public addresses from a pool. Cons: limited by pool size; not stable for inbound access.
PAT
Pros: Highly scalable for outbound users. Cons: No stable inbound identity; port mapping may complicate some services.
Practical ordering
Implement configurations in order of specificity: Static mappings first, then Dynamic pools, then PAT for remaining traffic. Routers process NAT rules such that specific static entries should not be masked by generic PAT rules.

screens.title: Troubleshooting NAT configurations
screens.narratorSegment: When NAT does not behave as expected, several recurring issues cause the problem. First, swapped interface roles where ip nat inside and ip nat outside are applied to the wrong interfaces will prevent translations — verify interface designations and their IP addresses first. Second, ACL misconfiguration used to select inside hosts for Dynamic NAT or PAT can be too broad or too restrictive; confirm that the access-list matches the intended source addresses. Third, overlapping address ranges between inside networks and outside global addresses or pools can cause routing ambiguity. Fourth, omitting the overload keyword when you expect PAT will consume pool addresses and cause rapid exhaustion. For verification use show ip nat translations to inspect active mappings and show ip nat statistics for resource usage. Use clear ip nat translation * to reset translations during testing; this helps reproduce translation behavior from a clean state. Use debug ip nat sparingly and only in controlled environments, because it can be C P U-intensive. When you see no translations, start with interface roles, then check ACLs, then pool definitions, and finally test with a clear followed by initiating traffic. A useful habit is to document expected translations and test one change at a time to isolate the cause. What is your first step when translations are missing?

Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Lab Walkthrough

Step-by-step template (Router R1)

Follow this sequence to configure Static NAT for a web server, Dynamic NAT for power users, and PAT for everyone else.

R1>enable
R1#configure terminal

! --- Interface Configuration ---
R1(config)#interface GigabitEthernet0/0
R1(config-if)#ip address 192.168.1.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)#ip nat inside
R1(config-if)#no shutdown
R1(config-if)#exit

R1(config)#interface GigabitEthernet0/1
R1(config-if)#ip address 203.0.113.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)#ip nat outside
R1(config-if)#no shutdown
R1(config-if)#exit

! --- Static NAT for Web Server ---
R1(config)#ip nat inside source static 192.168.1.10 203.0.113.10

! --- Dynamic NAT for Power Users ---
R1(config)#ip access-list standard DYNAMIC_NAT_ACL
R1(config-std-nacl)#permit 192.168.1.20 0.0.0.3
R1(config-std-nacl)#permit 192.168.1.24 0.0.0.1
R1(config-std-nacl)#exit

R1(config)#ip nat pool DYNAMIC_POOL 203.0.113.20 203.0.113.22 netmask 255.255.255.252
R1(config)#ip nat inside source list DYNAMIC_NAT_ACL pool DYNAMIC_POOL

! --- PAT for All Other Internal Users ---
R1(config)#ip access-list standard PAT_ACL
R1(config-std-nacl)#permit 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255
R1(config-std-nacl)#exit

R1(config)#ip nat inside source list PAT_ACL interface GigabitEthernet0/1 overload

R1(config)#end
R1#show ip nat translations
R1#show ip nat statistics
Verification
Use show ip nat translations to confirm static entries and dynamic allocations. Check statistics to ensure pool capacity and PAT usage are healthy.
Test plan
Test external access to the web server, simulate power-user sessions to exercise the pool, and validate many client sessions through PAT.

screens.title: Common NAT configuration mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: In practice several repeatable misconfigurations account for most NAT failures. One frequent error is assigning ip nat inside to the wrong interface; this stops translation entirely and is easy to detect by verifying interface roles. Another error is using ACLs that mistakenly exclude hosts that should be translated or that are too broad and include unintended traffic; always test ACL matches with packet captures or simple pings. Overlapping IP ranges between inside networks and outside global addresses or pools can create routing conflicts — avoid reusing ranges. Forgetting the overload keyword when intending PAT converts the behavior into dynamic NAT semantics and can exhaust pool resources. Also, placing NAT rules in the wrong order or creating conflicting static mappings that collide with dynamic pools will produce unexpected outcomes. For troubleshooting, follow a minimal checklist: confirm interface tags, review ACLs, inspect pool netmask and range, clear translations for a clean test, and only then use debug to capture translation events at the packet level. Remember that NAT is deterministic when configured correctly; careful documentation and ordered testing will prevent most issues. fullNarratorScript:
Network Address Translation is a pragmatic solution that lets private networks use non-routable addresses while communicating on the public internet. In practice, NAT conserves scarce IPv4 addresses and obscures internal topology by translating between inside local addresses and inside global addresses. You will learn the address role names, how a router uses ip nat inside and ip nat outside to decide which packets to translate, and the three operational patterns: Static NAT for stable one-to-one mappings, Dynamic NAT that borrows addresses from a pool, and PAT which overloads a single public address using unique source ports. Knowing when to use each type is critical: servers that must be reachable externally usually need Static NAT, small groups of hosts can use Dynamic NAT when limited public addresses are available, and most user internet access uses PAT for scale. This lesson also prepares you to configure, verify, and troubleshoot NAT on Cisco routers using commands like show ip nat translations and clear ip nat translation. By the end you will be able to map requirements to NAT types and reason about common misconfigurations that prevent translations. Think about a web server you must make reachable from the internet — NAT gives you a predictable public identity while keeping the server on a private network.

In this chapter you will build a practical skill set around NAT. First, you will explain why NAT is used and identify the address roles such as inside local and inside global. Second, you will differentiate Static NAT, Dynamic NAT, and PAT so you can pick the correct strategy for servers, power users, and general hosts. Third, you will configure Static mappings and Dynamic pools on a Cisco router, and implement PAT using the overload keyword. Finally, you will verify and troubleshoot NAT with show and debug commands. Each objective includes hands-on practice: for example, configuring a Static NAT mapping for a web server and verifying reachability. You'll also practice creating ACLs used for dynamic pools and PAT. These competencies matter because NAT influences connectivity and security at the network edge; mistakes commonly come from incorrect interface designations or ACL mismatches. By the end you will recognize configuration errors, interpret translation tables, and restore correct operation. This set of objectives prepares you to implement address translation reliably in production networks while conserving IPv4 addresses and maintaining predictable server presence.

This second objectives slide drills into configuration and verification skills. You will practice applying ip nat inside and ip nat outside consistently to interfaces so the router can correctly translate traffic. You will write standard access control lists to select which inside hosts are eligible for dynamic NAT or PAT. You will create NAT pools and understand netmask sizing so addresses match expected ranges. For verification, you will use show ip nat translations to observe active mappings and show ip nat statistics to confirm resource usage. For troubleshooting, you will use clear ip nat translation star to reset state during tests and consider debug ip nat carefully when needing packet-level detail. Each skill is backed by a short lab: map a web server with Static NAT, configure a small dynamic pool for power users, then enable PAT for the rest of the subnet. These operations teach order and specificity: static mappings are permanent, dynamic mappings come from a pool, and PAT requires overload. Knowing these rules avoids common errors in production. After practicing these objectives you will be prepared to build NAT rules that meet real world requirements and verify their impact.

Network Address Translation translates addresses used inside a private network into addresses usable on the public internet. The practical effect is twofold: it conserves IPv4 addresses and it separates internal addressing from the externally visible address space. For example, a company with thousands of devices can assign private addresses like 192.168.0.0/16 internally and use a small set of public addresses only when hosts initiate external sessions. This avoids the need to request a public address for every internal host. NAT also provides a modest layer of obscurity: external systems see the inside global addresses rather than the internal topology. That does not replace proper security controls, but it reduces direct exposure of internal hosts. Definition matters when choosing a strategy. Static NAT is a permanent one-to-one translation used when an internal service must be reachable by a stable public address. Dynamic NAT borrows addresses from a pool, which is useful when a subset of users occasionally need public addresses. PAT, or NAT Overload, multiplexes many internal hosts onto a single public IP using different source ports, which is why PAT is the dominant model for general internet access. A common misconception is that NAT is a security control — while NAT can hide internal addresses, it is not a substitute for firewalls and access controls. Consider how a web server keeps a known public presence via Static NAT: that predictability is the primary reason to choose static mapping for servers. How would you match your use case to one of these three types?

NAT uses specific names for the addresses involved in translation — learning these terms prevents confusion when designing and troubleshooting translations. Inside Local refers to a private IP assigned to a host within the internal network. Inside Global is the public IP that represents that internal host when it communicates externally. Outside Local is how an external host appears to the inside network; this could be unchanged or translated depending on the topology. Outside Global is the external host's public address on the internet. For example, an internal web server might be Inside Local 192.168.1.10; when you create a static mapping to 203.0.113.10, that public address is the Inside Global. If an internal client accesses an external service, the remote server's public address is the Outside Global and the router may show that same address as Outside Local to inside hosts. Misreading these roles often leads to troubleshooting errors, especially when examining show ip nat translations output. Remember: 'inside' and 'outside' are relative to the router performing NAT. A frequent mistake is assuming inside and outside always map to physical interfaces by name; instead verify which interfaces are tagged with ip nat inside and ip nat outside before relying on translations. How would you label the addresses in your network for clarity?

The router must know which interfaces face the internal and external networks to apply NAT correctly. The commands ip nat inside and ip nat outside tag interfaces so the NAT engine treats packets according to their direction. When an internal host initiates a connection to the internet, the packet arrives on an interface marked as inside; the router consults translation rules and either applies a static mapping, assigns an address from a dynamic pool, or performs PAT using the outside interface address with overload. If these interface tags are reversed, translation never occurs. For example, if you accidentally set the WAN-facing interface to ip nat inside, the router will not translate outbound traffic as expected and show ip nat translations will be empty. A straightforward process to avoid this error is to confirm interface addresses and then apply the ip nat keywords: set the inside-facing interface connected to 192.168.1.0/24 as ip nat inside and the outside-facing interface connected to 203.0.113.0/24 as ip nat outside. After configuration verify translations by initiating traffic and using show ip nat translations. A common troubleshooting step is repeating the interface checks first, because incorrect interface roles are among the most frequent causes of NAT failure. What would you check first if translations never appear?

Static NAT creates a permanent one-to-one mapping between an inside local IP and an inside global IP. Use this when an internal host, like a web or email server, must keep the same public address so external clients can reach it reliably. The configuration pattern sets the inside and outside interface roles, then applies ip nat inside source static. In the example from the chapter, the server 192.168.1.10 is mapped to 203.0.113.2. After creating the static mapping, incoming packets destined for 203.0.113.2 are translated and forwarded to the internal server. A common pitfall is forgetting to tag the router interfaces correctly; if ip nat inside is missing on the LAN interface or ip nat outside is missing on the WAN interface, the translation will not occur. Another mistake is overlapping mappings that conflict with dynamic pools or PAT rules; keep static mappings distinct. When verifying, use show ip nat translations to confirm the static entry and test external access to the public IP. A misconception is thinking Static NAT affects outbound source addresses for client connections; static mappings primarily ensure inbound reachability to the internal host. How would you prioritize static mappings when you also need a dynamic pool and PAT on the same router?

Dynamic NAT creates an on-demand mapping between eligible inside hosts and a pool of public IP addresses. Unlike Static NAT, mappings are temporary and only exist for the duration of a session. To configure Dynamic NAT you define a standard ACL identifying the inside addresses that may be translated, then declare an ip nat pool with the public addresses and netmask, and finally bind them with ip nat inside source list pool. In the chapter example, hosts in 192.168.1.0/24 can be dynamically assigned addresses from 203.0.113.10 through 203.0.113.15. If the pool is exhausted, subsequent internal requests fail until an address is freed. This limitation distinguishes Dynamic NAT from PAT, which can scale more densely. A common configuration error is a mismatched netmask for the pool or ACL too narrow or too broad; these mistakes either prevent translations or translate unintended hosts. For verification, watch show ip nat translations during session initiation to observe pool addresses assigned. A practical misconception is expecting Dynamic NAT to provide inbound stable access — it does not guarantee the same public IP is available for return traffic, so do not use it for servers that require consistent reachability. Would a small team of power users benefit more from Dynamic NAT than PAT? Consider pool size against concurrency.

Port Address Translation, commonly called PAT or NAT Overload, enables many internal hosts to share a single public IP address by differentiating sessions with unique source ports. To configure PAT you create a standard ACL that matches internal hosts, then use ip nat inside source list interface overload. The overload keyword signals the router to reuse the outside interface IP and vary source ports to maintain session uniqueness. In the chapter example, all hosts in 192.168.1.0/24 appear externally as 203.0.113.1 while the router tracks port mappings to maintain separate connections. PAT is highly scalable for general internet access, but it does not give an internal host a stable public identity; it is unsuitable for servers that need inbound connections mapped to them. A common error is omitting overload, which results in dynamic NAT behavior that can exhaust pool addresses quickly. When verifying PAT, use show ip nat translations to inspect port mappings and statistics. Misconceptions include assuming PAT hides all internal details; while it hides internal IPs, port-level mappings still reveal session endpoints.
